lead: Autopsy is a graphical program for examining a hard drive, disk image or mobile device and recovering evidence from it. It is built on The Sleuth Kit and other open source forensic tools.
use_when: You have a disk image and want to browse files, search for words and review web activity in one window.
You are learning forensics and want a free tool with a clear case workflow.
Several examiners need to work on the same case.

features.title: Cases and data sources
items: Creates a case, then adds one or more data sources to it
Data source types include disk image or VM file, local disk, logical files and unallocated space image file
Also accepts Autopsy Logical Imager results and XRY text exports
Works with a host name for each data source, so you can group sources by device

features.title: Ingest modules
items: Ingest modules run in the background after you add a data source
Hash Lookup calculates file hashes and checks them against hash sets
Keyword Search looks for words in the content of the data source
Recent Activity extracts web artifacts and other signs of user activity

features.title: Reviewing and searching
items: Tree viewer with Data Sources, Views and Results nodes
Searches by keyword, file attributes and common properties, and across cases
Specialised viewers: Image Gallery, Timeline, Communications Visualization, Geolocation and Personas
Tags and comments mark the items that matter

features.title: Reports
items: HTML and Excel reports of all results or only tagged results
CASE-UCO JSON file for one data source
Google Earth KML file from GPS data
Portable Case, which is a smaller Autopsy case holding tagged items

requirements: The project provides a Windows installer (.msi) and ZIP files for Linux and macOS. The user guide recommends at least 16 GB of RAM. By default Autopsy uses up to 4 GB of memory, and you can raise this in the options. Set your antivirus to skip the case folder, or it may remove results.

steps.title: Download and install
steps.text: Get the installer from the Autopsy download page. On Windows, run the .msi file and click through the dialogs until Finish. On Linux and macOS, the project provides ZIP files.

steps.title: Create a case
steps.text: On the Welcome screen click Create New Case, or use the Case menu and choose New Case Wizard. Enter a case name and a storage folder. Case number and examiner name are optional.

steps.title: Add a data source
steps.text: The Add Data Source wizard opens after the case is created. Choose a host, then the data source type. For an image, select the first file of the set. Work on a copy of the evidence, never the original.

steps.title: Choose ingest modules
steps.text: Select the modules to run. Use the Advanced button on a module to add hash sets or keyword lists. A progress bar in the lower right shows the work. You can start browsing while modules are still running.

steps.title: Review the results
steps.text: Use the tree on the left. Web activity is under Results, Extracted Data. Matches against hash sets are under Results, Hashset Hits. The Ingest Inbox lists recent findings. Right-click a file to extract it.

steps.title: Tag items of interest
steps.text: Right-click a file or result and add a tag or comment. Tags are what you will use to build the report, so tag as you go and add a short note on why each item matters.

steps.title: Generate a report
steps.text: Click Generate Report on the toolbar. Pick a report type such as HTML or Excel, choose the data sources and tags, and run it. Finished reports are listed under the Reports node at the bottom of the tree.

cases.title: General disk examination
cases.why: Browse the file system, see deleted files and view file content and metadata in one place.

cases.title: Web and user activity
cases.why: The Recent Activity module collects web artifacts so you can review what a user did on a computer.

cases.title: Known file filtering
cases.why: Hash sets let you flag known files of interest or set known files aside.

cases.title: Keyword investigations
cases.why: Keyword Search indexes the content so you can look for names, words and phrases across the whole image.

cases.title: Team casework
cases.why: Multi-user mode lets several examiners work on one case. It needs extra server setup described in the user guide.

cases.title: Teaching and practice
cases.why: It is free and has a guided workflow, so students can practise on test images.

strengths: One window for browsing, searching, timeline, geolocation and reporting.
Reads common image formats such as raw, E01, VMDK and VHD.
Detailed user documentation is published for each version.
Third-party ingest modules can be installed.
limits: Large images take a long time to process, and the user guide recommends at least 16 GB of RAM.
Keyword search depends on indexing, so searches may be incomplete until the Keyword Search module has finished.
The Linux and macOS packages are ZIP files, and the installation page gives no step-by-step setup for them, so beginners may need extra help.
It examines evidence that already exists. You need another tool to make the disk image first.
Antivirus software can interfere with the case folder.
Multi-user cases need a server cluster, which is more work to set up.
Results depend on which ingest modules you chose, so a missed setting can mean missed evidence.

works_with.note: The command-line toolkit that Autopsy is built on
Create the disk image on Linux
Hash sets for the Hash Lookup module
A second tool to cross-check important findings
Build a wider super timeline from the same evidence
